274				fmt.Fprintf(out, "[watch] short-term memory updated (%d records from %d changed transcripts)\n", stats.Records, stats.Files)
275				if stats.Failed > 0 {
276					fmt.Fprintf(out, "[watch] short-term memory incomplete: %d transcripts failed to scan; consolidation will repair\n", stats.Failed)
277				}
278			}
279		}
280		// Delta state is itself a source-change signal. Do this before the git
281		// fingerprint gate so a changed/failed/overflowed export is never stranded
282		// in the short-term overlay waiting for an unrelated commit or restart.
283		if deltaNeedsReconcile && steps.reconcile != nil {
284			if err := steps.reconcile(ctx); err != nil {
285				fmt.Fprintf(out, "[watch] memory reconciliation failed (durable overlay retained): %v\n", err)
286			} else {
287				fmt.Fprintln(out, "[watch] long-term memory reconciliation queued")
288			}
289		}
290		cursor := loadWatchCursor(cursorPath)
291		// The hosted step pulls teammates' facts as much as it publishes local
292		// ones, so it must run on idle (no-change) ticks too — a machine that only
293		// receives would otherwise never sync. The defer below makes it run on
294		// every exit path from here down, including a failed refresh: a failed
295		// refresh never advances the main cursor, so a machine whose refresh
296		// always fails (e.g. the graph plugin is missing) takes that path on every
297		// tick and would otherwise be starved of the team's facts forever
298		// (COR-2114; a hand-placed call per return had already missed a path
299		// twice). It is token-free and throttled by its own cursor timestamp,
300		// advanced regardless of outcome so a failing hosted endpoint cannot turn
301		// every tick into an egress attempt. The success path still calls it
302		// explicitly BEFORE the agent steps — the `ran` guard makes the deferred
303		// call a no-op then — so the sync never inherits a context cancelled
304		// during a long agent step and burns its throttle window on an attempt
305		// that never happened.
306		factsSyncRan := false
307		runFactsSync := func() {
308			if factsSyncRan {
309				return
310			}
311			factsSyncRan = true
312			now := steps.now().UTC()
313			if steps.factsSync == nil || now.Sub(cursor.LastFactsSyncAt) < hostedSyncMinInterval {
314				return
315			}
316			attempted, err := steps.factsSync(ctx)
317			switch {
318			case err != nil:
319				fmt.Fprintf(out, "[watch] hosted fact sync failed (local brain unaffected): %v\n", err)
320			case attempted:
321				fmt.Fprintln(out, "[watch] hosted fact sync ran")
322			}
323			markFactsSyncAttempt(cursorPath, now)
324		}
325		defer runFactsSync()
326		fp := steps.fingerprint(ctx)
327		changed := fp != cursor.LastFingerprint || cursor.LastRefreshAt.IsZero()
328		if !changed && !(cursor.PendingSeed && w.seedAgent != "none" || cursor.PendingDistill && w.distill) {
329			fmt.Fprintln(out, "[watch] no change; nothing to do")
330			return
331		}
332		// Consolidation throttle: the fingerprint includes checkpoint refs, so an
333		// active agent session flips it every turn; without a throttle the heavy
334		// full refresh would run every tick exactly when the machine is busiest.
335		// A failed delta means nothing carried the new work, so the full refresh is
336		// the repair path and must not wait the whole interval (Bugbot PR #78),
337		// but it is throttled too, just on a shorter clock. The delta and the full
338		// refresh contend for the SAME brain write lock, so an unthrottled repair
339		// would fire the heavy path every tick for as long as the delta keeps
340		// failing, contending for the very lock that broke it. watchRepairWait
341		// escalates after one tick and then backs off to the normal cadence. An
342		// overflowed buffer still forces consolidation immediately: recall
343		// completeness is at risk, and a successful consolidation clears the
344		// overlay, so it cannot repeat the way a failing delta can. The first ever
345		// refresh always runs.
346		if changed && w.consolidateEvery > 0 && !cursor.LastRefreshAt.IsZero() && !bufferFull {
347			wait := w.consolidateEvery
348			state := "short-term memory is current"
349			if !deltaHealthy {
350				wait = watchRepairWait(w, cursor.ConsolidationRepairs)
351				state = fmt.Sprintf("short-term memory failed; repair refresh backing off after %d consecutive repairs", cursor.ConsolidationRepairs)
352			}
353			if since := steps.now().UTC().Sub(cursor.LastRefreshAt); since < wait {
354				fmt.Fprintf(out, "[watch] consolidation deferred (%s since last full refresh; due in %s; %s)\n",
355					since.Round(time.Second), (wait - since).Round(time.Second), state)
356				return
357			}
358		}
359		if changed {
360			if err := steps.refresh(ctx); err != nil {
361				// Refresh failed: do NOT spend tokens on an unrefreshed brain, and do NOT advance the cursor.
362				// The next tick retries the free refresh before attempting pending agent work.
363				fmt.Fprintf(out, "[watch] refresh failed (skipping agent work this tick): %v\n", err)
364				return
365			}
366		}
367		runFactsSync()
368		reserved, reason, err := reserveWatchAgentSpend(cursorPath, fp, w, agentCalls, steps.now().UTC(), !deltaHealthy)
369		if err != nil {
370			fmt.Fprintf(out, "[watch] cursor update failed (skipping agent work this tick): %v\n", err)
371			return
372		}
373		if changed {
374			fmt.Fprintln(out, "[watch] refreshed (deterministic, no agent tokens)")
375		}
376	
377		if !w.agentWorkEnabled() {
378			return
379		}
380		if !reserved {
381			fmt.Fprintf(out, "[watch] agent work skipped: %s\n", reason)
382			return
383		}
384		// Gated token-spending work: agent seed synthesis and/or distill, at most once per --distill-every,
385		// counted against --budget. A transient failure of one step is intentionally best-effort: we still
386		// advance the spend cursor + budget below so a failed step retries on the NEXT interval, not every
387		// tick (and a step that already burned tokens before failing can't be re-run for free).
388		pending := loadWatchCursor(cursorPath)
389		seedDone, distillDone := false, false
390		seedAttempted := false
391		if w.seedAgent != "none" && pending.PendingSeed {
392			seedAttempted = true
393			if err := steps.seed(ctx); err != nil {
394				fmt.Fprintf(out, "[watch] seed synthesis failed: %v\n", err)
395			} else {
396				seedDone = true
397				fmt.Fprintln(out, "[watch] synthesized seed (agent step; spent tokens)")
398			}
399		}
400		if w.distill && pending.PendingDistill {
401			switch err := steps.distill(ctx); {
402			case errors.Is(err, errDistillPassBusy):
403				// When distill was the only agent step, nothing was spent, so nothing
404				// may be charged. Hand the window
405				// back instead of logging "spent tokens" and going quiet until the
406				// next one — otherwise a watcher installed beside `setup`'s
407				// hours-long backfill loses its first window (and, if the backfill
408				// outlives it, every window) to a pass that never ran.
409				// A seed step attempted immediately before this may already have spent
410				// tokens even when it returned an error, so its reservation must stay.
411				if seedAttempted {
412					fmt.Fprintln(out, "[watch] distill skipped: another pass holds this brain; the spend window remains consumed by seed synthesis")
413				} else {
414					releaseWatchAgentSpend(cursorPath, cursor.LastAgentSpendAt, agentCalls)
415					fmt.Fprintln(out, "[watch] distill skipped: another pass holds this brain; the spend window was NOT consumed")
416				}
417			case errors.Is(err, errDistillDeferred):
418				fmt.Fprintln(out, "[watch] distilled capped batch; remaining sessions pending for the next spend window")
419			case err != nil:
420				fmt.Fprintf(out, "[watch] distill failed: %v\n", err)
421			default:
422				distillDone = true
423				fmt.Fprintln(out, "[watch] distilled facts (agent step; spent tokens)")
424			}
425		}
426		if err := withWatchCursorLock(cursorPath, func() error {
427			current := loadWatchCursor(cursorPath)
428			// A newer refresh owns its own pending work.
429			if current.LastFingerprint != pending.LastFingerprint || !current.LastRefreshAt.Equal(pending.LastRefreshAt) {
430				return nil
431			}
432			if seedDone {
433				current.PendingSeed = false
434			}
435			if distillDone {
436				current.PendingDistill = false
437			}
438			return saveWatchCursor(cursorPath, current)
439		}); err != nil {
440			fmt.Fprintf(out, "[watch] completion cursor update failed: %v\n", err)
441		}
442	}
443	
444	// releaseWatchAgentSpend gives back a window reserved by reserveWatchAgentSpend
445	// when the gated step turned out to do nothing at all. previous is the
446	// LastAgentSpendAt read at the top of this tick, so the cursor lands exactly
447	// where it was; the budget counter is decremented for the same reason. Failures
448	// are deliberately silent: the worst case is the pre-existing behaviour (a
449	// window charged for a no-op), and a watcher must never die on cursor
450	// bookkeeping.
451	func releaseWatchAgentSpend(cursorPath string, previous time.Time, agentCalls *int) {
452		_ = withWatchCursorLock(cursorPath, func() error {
453			cursor := loadWatchCursor(cursorPath)
454			cursor.LastAgentSpendAt = previous
455			if *agentCalls > 0 {
456				*agentCalls--
457			}
458			return saveWatchCursor(cursorPath, cursor)
459		})
460	}

462	// agentWorkEnabled reports whether any token-spending step is turned on.
463	func (w watchCommandOptions) agentWorkEnabled() bool {
464		return w.distill || w.seedAgent != "none"

467	// watchStepsForRepo builds the per-repo side effects the watch loop drives. refresh is ALWAYS the free
468	// (seed-agent none) deterministic refresh; seed and distill are the gated token steps. Shared by the
469	// single-repo `watch` and the workspace fan-out so both stay token-frugal the same way.
470	func watchStepsForRepo(cmd *cobra.Command, opts Options, w watchCommandOptions, repoDir string, now func() time.Time) watchSteps {
471		return watchSteps{
472			now:         now,
473			fingerprint: func(c context.Context) string { return watchFingerprint(c, opts.Runner, repoDir) },
474			delta:       func(c context.Context) (shortTermStats, error) { return watchShortTermDelta(c, cmd, opts, repoDir) },
475			reconcile: func(c context.Context) error {
476				_, warning, err := reconcileMemoryAndLaunch(c, opts, repoDir, "watch")
477				if warning != "" {
478					fmt.Fprintf(cmd.ErrOrStderr(), "warning: memory coordinator: %s\n", warning)
479				}
480				return err
481			},
482			refresh: func(c context.Context) error { return watchDeterministicRefresh(c, cmd, opts, repoDir) },
483			seed:    func(c context.Context) error { return watchSeed(c, cmd, opts, w, repoDir) },
484			distill: func(c context.Context) error { return watchDistill(c, cmd, opts, w, repoDir) },
485			factsSync: func(c context.Context) (bool, error) {
486				storage, err := repoStoragePaths(c, opts.Runner, opts.Env, repoDir)
487				if err != nil {
488					return false, err
489				}
490				branch := hostedSyncBranch(c, opts.Runner, repoDir)
491				attempted, err := hostedFactsSyncAndPull(c, cmd.ErrOrStderr(), opts, repoDir, storage, branch)
492				if err != nil {
493					return attempted, err
494				}
495				if branch != distillDefaultBranch {
496					also, err := hostedFactsSyncAndPull(c, cmd.ErrOrStderr(), opts, repoDir, storage, distillDefaultBranch)
497					return attempted || also, err
498				}
499				return attempted, nil
500			},
501			paused: func() bool { return backgroundPaused(opts.Env) },
502		}
503	}

530	// watchShouldSpend decides whether the token-spending agent work (seed and/or distill) runs this tick:
531	// only when at least one is enabled AND --distill-every has elapsed since the last agent spend
532	// (cursor-tracked across restarts) AND the --budget cap is not yet reached. This is the structural
533	// token-frugality guarantee — it bounds seed synthesis exactly like distill.
534	func watchShouldSpend(w watchCommandOptions, cursor watchCursor, agentCalls int, now time.Time) (bool, string) {
535		if !w.agentWorkEnabled() {
536			return false, "no agent steps enabled"
537		}
538		if !(cursor.LastAgentSpendAt.IsZero() || now.Sub(cursor.LastAgentSpendAt) >= w.distillEvery) {
539			return false, "--distill-every not elapsed"
540		}
541		if w.budget > 0 && agentCalls >= w.budget {
542			return false, fmt.Sprintf("--budget %d reached", w.budget)
543		}
544		return true, ""
545	}

547	// watchRepairWait is the minimum time between full consolidations while the
548	// short-term delta is failing. It starts at one tick (a transient delta failure
549	// repairs on the very next pass) and doubles per consecutive repair up to the
550	// normal --consolidate-every, so a persistently failing delta degrades to the
551	// ordinary consolidation cadence instead of thrashing the shared brain write
552	// lock on every tick.
553	func watchRepairWait(w watchCommandOptions, repairs int) time.Duration {
554		wait := w.interval
555		if wait <= 0 {
556			wait = time.Minute
557		}
558		if repairs > watchRepairBackoffMax {
559			repairs = watchRepairBackoffMax
560		}
561		for i := 0; i < repairs && wait < w.consolidateEvery; i++ {
562			wait *= 2
563		}
564		if wait > w.consolidateEvery {
565			wait = w.consolidateEvery
566		}
567		return wait
568	}

570	// reserveWatchAgentSpend advances the refresh cursor after a successful full
571	// refresh and decides whether the gated token work may run. repair reports
572	// whether THIS refresh ran early because the short-term delta failed; it drives
573	// the watchRepairWait backoff and is cleared by the first healthy delta.
574	func reserveWatchAgentSpend(cursorPath, fingerprint string, w watchCommandOptions, agentCalls *int, now time.Time, repair bool) (bool, string, error) {
575		var cursor watchCursor
576		var reserved bool
577		var reason string
578		err := withWatchCursorLock(cursorPath, func() error {
579			cursor = loadWatchCursor(cursorPath)
580			changed := fingerprint != cursor.LastFingerprint || cursor.LastRefreshAt.IsZero()
581			if changed {
582				cursor.PendingSeed = cursor.PendingSeed || w.seedAgent != "none"
583				cursor.PendingDistill = cursor.PendingDistill || w.distill
584				cursor.LastFingerprint = fingerprint
585				cursor.LastRefreshAt = now
586				if repair {
587					if cursor.ConsolidationRepairs < watchRepairBackoffMax {
588						cursor.ConsolidationRepairs++
589					}
590				} else {
591					cursor.ConsolidationRepairs = 0
592				}
593			}
594			if !w.agentWorkEnabled() {
595				if changed {
596					return saveWatchCursor(cursorPath, cursor)
597				}
598				return nil
599			}
600			ok, skipReason := watchShouldSpend(w, cursor, *agentCalls, now)
601			if !ok {
602				reason = skipReason
603				if changed {
604					return saveWatchCursor(cursorPath, cursor)
605				}
606				return nil
607			}
608			cursor.LastAgentSpendAt = now
609			*agentCalls++
610			reserved = true
611			return saveWatchCursor(cursorPath, cursor)
612		})
613		return reserved, reason, err
614	}

616	func withWatchCursorLock(cursorPath string, fn func() error) error {
617		root := filepath.Dir(cursorPath)
618		if info, err := os.Lstat(root); err == nil && info.Mode()&os.ModeSymlink != 0 {
619			return fmt.Errorf("watch cursor directory must not be a symlink: %s", root)
620		} else if err != nil && !os.IsNotExist(err) {
621			return err
622		}
623		if err := rejectExistingSymlinkPathComponents(root, brainLockDirName); err != nil {
624			return err
625		}
626		lock, err := acquireFileLock(filepath.Join(root, brainLockDirName, watchCursorLockName), "watch_locked", brainWriteLockTimeout)
627		if err != nil {
628			return err
629		}
630		defer func() { _ = lock.Close() }()
631		return fn()
632	}

634	// watchFingerprint is a token-free change signal: the local checkpoint ref, the fetched (origin)
635	// checkpoint ref, and the worktree HEAD. Including the origin ref means a `git fetch` that brings in
636	// checkpoint activity from elsewhere also triggers a refresh. When all are unchanged since the cursor,
637	// there is nothing new to ingest.
638	func watchFingerprint(ctx context.Context, runner CommandRunner, repoDir string) string {
639		rev := func(ref string) string {
640			if runner == nil {
641				return ""
642			}
643			out, _, err := runner.Run(ctx, repoDir, "git", "rev-parse", "--verify", "--quiet", ref)
644			if err != nil {
645				return ""
646			}
647			return strings.TrimSpace(string(out))
648		}
649		return rev(v1MainRef) + ":" + rev(v1OriginRef) + ":" + rev("HEAD")
650	}

653	// agent ALWAYS "none", then durably reconciles long-term conversation work.
654	// The coordinator owns projection publication, retries, and crash recovery;
655	// watch only nudges it. Agent seed synthesis remains a separate gated step.
656	func watchDeterministicRefresh(ctx context.Context, cmd *cobra.Command, opts Options, repoDir string) error {
657		return watchDeterministicRefreshComponents(ctx, cmd, opts, repoDir, watchTickBuildsHistoryProjection, false, nil)

660	// watchDeterministicRefreshComponents runs the free refresh with explicit failure
661	// policy and an optional outcome observer. Setup chooses best effort; ticks fail fast.
662	//
663	// historyIndex separates the two callers that were previously identical. A
664	// watch TICK passes false: it runs every few minutes, the per-tick delta
665	// already makes new conversations recallable, and the coordinator consolidates
666	// the durable projection on its own schedule. `setup` passes true, because it
667	// is a one-shot onboarding build (the same shape as a manual `refresh`, which
668	// has always defaulted history on) and it ends by telling the user to run
669	// `entire-brain brief`. With history unbuilt that brief silently drops its
670	// transcript half and prints "history index missing" instead — setup's own
671	// recommended next command, answering with a warning about setup's own output.
672	// watchDeterministicRefreshOptions is the free path's refresh configuration,
673	// built here rather than inline so both callers' intent — above all whether the
674	// history projection is built — is readable and testable in one place.
675	func watchDeterministicRefreshOptions(historyIndex bool) refreshCommandOptions {
676		return refreshCommandOptions{
677			outputDir:       defaultExportDir,
678			checkpointLimit: defaultCheckpointLimit,
679			entireBinary:    "entire",
680			graphBinary:     "entire",
681			scope:           exportScopeAll,
682			// A tick must not bypass the durable work ledger: the per-tick delta
683			// already makes new conversations recallable while the coordinator
684			// consolidates asynchronously. A one-shot onboarding build has no next
685			// tick to wait for, so `setup` asks for it explicitly.
686			historyIndex: historyIndex,
687			semantic:     true,
688			seed: seedCommandOptions{
689				includeTests:       true,
690				maxFileBytes:       defaultSeedMaxFileBytes,
691				maxFiles:           defaultSeedMaxFiles,
692				format:             "markdown+json",
693				agent:              "none", // free: deterministic seed only; agent seed is gated via watchSeed
694				agentQuickTimeout:  2 * time.Minute,
695				agentDeepTimeout:   10 * time.Minute,
696				agentTimeoutAction: "keep-quick",
697				agentMaxInputBytes: defaultAgentMaxInput,
698			},
699		}
700	}

702	func watchDeterministicRefreshComponents(ctx context.Context, cmd *cobra.Command, opts Options, repoDir string, historyIndex, bestEffort bool, component func(name string, err error)) error {
703		perRepo := opts
704		perRepo.Env.RepoRoot = repoDir
705		refreshOpts := watchDeterministicRefreshOptions(historyIndex)
706		refreshOpts.component = component
707		refreshOpts.bestEffort = bestEffort
708		sub := &cobra.Command{}
709		sub.SetContext(ctx)
710		sub.SetOut(cmd.OutOrStdout())
711		sub.SetErr(cmd.ErrOrStderr())
712		if err := runRefresh(ctx, sub, perRepo, refreshOpts); err != nil {
713			return err
714		}
715		// Deterministic and token-free, like everything else in this step: index any
716		// checkpoint commits that landed since the entity index's high-water mark.
717		// Bounded and failure-silent — a missing `entire graph` provider must never
718		// fail a tick that otherwise refreshed the brain. Under a reporter it is one
719		// more degradable component, so `setup --json`, `status` and `doctor` can
720		// name it instead of losing the reason to a discarded stderr line; with no
721		// reporter the strict watch path keeps its warning and carries on exactly as
722		// before.
723		entityErr := refreshEntityIndexQuietly(ctx, perRepo, repoDir)
724		switch {
725		case component != nil:
726			component(brainComponentEntities, entityErr)
727		case entityErr != nil:
728			fmt.Fprintf(cmd.ErrOrStderr(), "warning: entity index refresh skipped: %v\n", entityErr)
729		}
730		_, warning, err := reconcileMemoryAndLaunch(ctx, perRepo, repoDir, "watch")
731		if warning != "" {
732			fmt.Fprintf(cmd.ErrOrStderr(), "warning: memory coordinator: %s\n", warning)
733		}
734		if component != nil {
735			component(brainComponentMemory, err)
736		}
737		if bestEffort {
738			return nil
739		}
740		return err
741	}

768	// errDistillPassBusy reports that the gated distill did NOTHING because another
769	// process already held the brain's distill pass lock. `distill` itself treats
770	// that as success — someone else is doing the work — but the watcher must not:
771	// it had already reserved the --distill-every window, so a silent success burned
772	// a whole window (24h by default) on a no-op and logged "spent tokens". `setup`
773	// creates that collision by design, spawning an hours-long detached backfill and
774	// installing a watcher that ticks immediately after.
775	var errDistillPassBusy = errors.New("another distill pass holds this brain")
776	
777	// errDistillDeferred retains pending work after a capped successful pass.
778	var errDistillDeferred = errors.New("distill has budget-deferred sessions")
779	
780	func watchDistill(ctx context.Context, cmd *cobra.Command, opts Options, w watchCommandOptions, repoDir string) error {
781		distillOpts := watchDistillOptions(w)
782		busy := false
783		deferred := false
784		distillOpts.onDeferredSessions = func(n int) { deferred = n > 0 }
785		distillOpts.onPassSkipped = func() { busy = true }
786		sub := &cobra.Command{}

87	// backfillRunning answers "is the detached backfill this repo recorded STILL
88	// running", which is the question both `setup`'s re-entrancy guard and `status`
89	// actually ask. processAlive alone cannot answer it.

91	// processAlive is a bare kill(pid, 0): it asks whether SOMETHING owns that pid,
92	// not whether it is our child. Pids are reused, and a reboot reuses low ones
93	// almost immediately — so a setup.json written before a reboot names a pid that
94	// after the reboot belongs to a system daemon. processAlive says true, `setup`

I'm designing the self-restart mechanism: capturing the binary's identity at loop start and checking for changes on each supervision pass, so that when the on-disk binary is upgraded, the daemon can detect it and trigger a restart.

I'm working out the handoff — rather than performing the restart inline, supervisedWatchLoop should return a sentinel when it detects a stale binary, letting the caller in runSupervisedWatch perform the actual restart. For the restart logic itself, I need to resolve the daemon's label and unit path, falling back to the default name, then rebuild the daemon plan using the current OS and binary path to drive the relaunch.

I'm also reasoning about when staleness checks should even apply — only when this process is actually running as the installed service (detectable via its log file or the presence of a daemon log maintainer), so a foreground `workspace watch` run by hand isn't affected. On macOS with launchd, the restart would spawn a detached shell that boots the service out and back in again, since bootout would otherwise kill this very process mid-restart; I'm weighing the ordering and exit-code edge cases around that handoff.

Restart=always covers exit 0 too, so that's safe. If spawn fails, logging and returning nil just lets launchd's KeepAlive retry, which is no worse than the current behavior and self-heals once the verbs update. The ordering matters though — bootout must fire before bootstrap so we never have two instances racing, and since bootout kills the old process first, no extra sleep is needed before spawning the new one.

For the Linux path, the same staleness check applies but the restart action is simply exiting, since systemd handles respawning the new binary. Windows has no supported manager, so staleness detection is gated off entirely and there's no risk from unsupported syscalls.

For detecting a stale binary, I'm comparing path, size, mtime, and using os.SameFile for inode-level comparison, wrapped in a watcher function that returns a boolean check.

On stat errors, I'm treating them as "unchanged" since atomic renames mean the file shouldn't disappear mid-replace; a non-atomic copy would show a changed mtime/size, which could cause bootstrapping a half-written binary, but that's acceptable since launchd's KeepAlive would just retry after a crash. I'm skipping debounce logic since the relink is atomic anyway.

For install/uninstallDaemon on darwin, I'm switching to bootout/bootstrap semantics with gui/<uid>: bootout ignoring errors, then bootstrap with error checking. But I realize the old `unload -w` in uninstallDaemon actually sets the service's Disabled flag, which would cause a subsequent bootstrap to fail with an EPERM-like "disabled" error — so I need to account for that disabled-state issue when reinstalling after an uninstall.

I'm also now worried about how to get the uid reliably, since os.Getuid() returns -1 on Windows and the install/uninstall functions need to stay testable across platforms with a fake runner, meaning expected uid values would vary by machine during tests.

So I should check how existing daemon setup tests handle the launchctl domain string to see if they already compute uid consistently rather than hardcoding it.

content.text:
**COR-2174 fixed and committed** (`42387ea0` on `cor-2174-watch-daemon-wedged`, 9 files, +331/−37).

What changed:

- **Daemon self-restart** (`internal/cli/watch_binary.go`, `workspace.go`): the supervised loop probes its executable every pass (inode + mtime + size) and exits with a clear log line when it was replaced. The probe only runs when the process is the installed service (reuses the stdout-is-the-unit-log identity test), so foreground runs are untouched.
- **Codesigning pin cleared**: before exiting on macOS, the daemon spawns a detached `launchctl bootout → enable → bootstrap` helper — plain exit would hit launchd's pinned cdhash (`OS_REASON_CODESIGNING`). On Linux, exit alone suffices (`Restart=always`).
- **`installDaemon`/`uninstallDaemon`** switched from legacy `unload`/`load -w` to `bootout`/`enable`/`bootstrap`, so a plain `setup` also heals a wedged machine. `enable` covers labels an older build's `unload -w` left disabled.
- **Honest liveness probe**: `launchctl list <label>` exits 0 for a registered-but-dead job, so `daemonRunning` now requires a PID entry. This fixes the "daemon ✓ running while every spawn failed" half of the ticket and makes setup's idempotence check fall through to a reinstall exactly in the wedged state. (This also overlaps COR-2162.)

- The live launchd sequence wasn't exercised end-to-end here (tests use a fake runner); `bootout`+`bootstrap` is the sequence you verified manually in the ticket. Worth watching the first real nightly rollover.
- Residual gap: if the daemon *crashes* after an upgrade but before its next pass, launchd's stale pin still blocks respawn until `setup` runs or next login. Accepted as rare; the upgrade path itself is now self-healing.

input.command:
gh pr create --base main --title "fix(watch): restart the supervised daemon when its binary is replaced" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Fixes COR-2174.

## Why

The installed watcher outlives the binary it was started from. After a rebuild, the old daemon's writer-path manifest load correctly refuses fields the new build added (`json: unknown field "transcript_storage"`), so every tick fails forever — distill never runs — while `entire brain status` still says `daemon ✓ running`. Restarting isn't enough on macOS either: launchd pins the cdhash of the ad-hoc-signed binary at registration, so after an upgrade every respawn fails with `OS_REASON_CODESIGNING` until the agent is re-registered.

## What changed

- The supervised loop probes its executable (inode + mtime + size) at the top of every pass and exits with a clear log line when it was replaced; the service manager then restarts it on the current build. The probe is active only for the installed service (stdout-is-the-unit-log identity test), so foreground `workspace watch` runs keep their behavior.
- Before exiting on darwin, the daemon re-registers itself through a detached `launchctl bootout` → `enable` → `bootstrap` helper — the sequence verified to re-record launchd's cdhash pin. On linux a plain exit suffices (`Restart=always`).
- `installDaemon`/`uninstallDaemon` switched from legacy `unload`/`load -w` to `bootout`/`enable`/`bootstrap`, so a plain `setup` also heals a wedged machine. `enable` clears the disabled flag an older build's `unload -w` may have recorded.
- `daemonRunning` now requires a PID entry in `launchctl list <label>` output: a registered-but-dead job (the wedged state) lists successfully, and equating registration with running is what hid the outage. `status` now reports "installed but not running", and setup's idempotence check falls through to a reinstall exactly then. Overlaps COR-2162.

## Validation

- New tests: binary-change probe (rewrite, rename-over, mid-replace vanish), supervised-loop exit on a stale binary, PID-based liveness.
- Full `go test ./...` passes; `gofmt -s` / `go vet` clean; windows and linux cross-builds OK.
- Not exercised here: the live launchd bootout/bootstrap sequence (tests use a fake runner); it is the workaround verified by hand in COR-2174.

## Known residual gap

If the daemon crashes after an upgrade but before its next pass, launchd's stale pin still blocks respawn until `setup` runs or the next login. Accepted as rare; the upgrade path itself is now self-healing.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -2

content.text:
# Review PR

Review a pull request with structured, actionable feedback.

## Arguments

- `` — PR number, URL, or branch name. If empty, review the current branch's open PR.

## Process

### 1. Fetch PR context

```
gh pr view <pr> --json title,body,baseRefName,headRefName,additions,deletions,changedFiles,commits,author
gh pr diff <pr>
```

Read the PR description carefully — it defines scope and intent. Everything you review should be evaluated against what the PR is trying to accomplish.

### 2. Understand the change

Before reviewing line-by-line:
- What is this PR doing and why?
- What files are touched and what's the blast radius?
- Are there any architectural implications?

### 3. Review with this checklist

**Correctness**
- Does the code do what the PR description says?
- Are there logic errors, off-by-one bugs, or unhandled edge cases?
- Are error paths handled correctly?

**Security**
- Any injection risks (SQL, XSS, command injection)?
- Are secrets, tokens, or credentials handled safely?
- Are inputs validated at system boundaries?

**Testing**
- Are there tests for the new/changed behavior?
- Do tests cover edge cases, not just the happy path?
- Are test assertions meaningful (not just "doesn't throw")?

**Design**
- Does the change follow existing codebase patterns and conventions?
- Is the abstraction level appropriate (not over/under-engineered)?
- Are there unnecessary changes outside the stated scope?

**Performance**
- Any N+1 queries, unbounded loops, or missing pagination?
- Are there opportunities for batching or caching that were missed?
- Will this scale with the data sizes it will encounter?

**Readability**
- Are names clear and consistent with the codebase?
- Is complex logic adequately explained?
- Would a future reader understand the "why" behind non-obvious decisions?

### 4. Adversarial review

Take a second, adversarial pass over the diff. Actively try to break the change — assume it has flaws and hunt for them across:

- **Performance** — worst-case inputs, hot paths, allocations, contention.
- **Stability** — race conditions, partial failures, retries, resource leaks, crash recovery.
- **Correctness** — inputs and states that violate the author's assumptions.
- **Simplicity** — code that could be deleted or replaced with something simpler/stdlib.
- **Platform design standards** — deviations from the platform's established design patterns and conventions.

Add any findings to the output using the same severity format.

### 5. Run /simplify

Run the `/simplify` skill (via the Skill tool) against the changed code and fold its findings into the review output.

### 6. Structure your output

For each finding, use this format:

**[severity] file:line — short title**
Description of the issue and why it matters. Include a suggested fix when possible.

Severity levels:
- **[blocking]** — Must fix before merge. Correctness bugs, security issues, data loss risks.
- **[important]** — Should fix. Design problems, missing tests for critical paths, performance issues.
- **[nit]** — Nice to fix. Style, naming, minor improvements. Don't block merge on these.
- **[question]** — Not necessarily wrong, but needs clarification or discussion.

### 7. Summary

End with a brief summary:
- Overall assessment (approve / request changes / needs discussion)
- What the PR does well
- Top 1-3 items that need attention
- Any scope concerns (changes that seem unrelated to the stated goal)

## Guidelines

- Review what's in the diff, not what you wish was there. Don't request unrelated refactoring.
- If the PR is large, focus on the most impactful files first.
- Be specific — "this could be better" is not useful. Show what "better" looks like.
- Distinguish between "this is wrong" and "I would do this differently." Only the former is blocking.
- If you're unsure about something, use [question] severity instead of asserting it's wrong.
- Read relevant source files (not just the diff) when you need context about how changed code integrates with the rest of the system.

Since I'm reviewing my own PR, I need to be genuinely adversarial rather than rubber-stamping it. I'll fetch the fresh diff, do a critical pass, consider delegating a second opinion to avoid anchoring on my own conclusions, then run /simplify before giving structured output.

One risk area I want to dig into carefully is the relaunchInstalledDaemon logic — specifically whether the bootout/bootstrap sequence races with launchd's KeepAlive respawn, since the daemon exits before the helper swaps the binary, which could leave the job in a failed-spawn state before the re-bootstrap lands.

Looking past that, I'm also checking whether the stale-binary error gets swallowed too quietly, whether the stale-probe gating inside the supervised loop runs correctly on the first pass, and whether the PID-check string matching for launchctl output could false-positive on other keys like "PIDSuffix" instead of the actual running "PID" field.

I'm also second-guessing whether the systemd path is unaffected by these changes, and whether the new "registered but not running" detail string could be mistaken for an error elsewhere since the full test suite already passed — I want to trace how that detail field actually gets used in status rendering.

There's a bigger concern with how the unit plan is built: if the watch plan is unreadable due to a schema mismatch, relaunch gets skipped and the daemon just exits, which could leave launchd stuck respawning until setup runs again — annoying but tolerable since it's logged. More worrying is that the daemon's own environment plist doesn't carry the ENTIRE_BRAIN_DAEMON_DIR variable, only plugin-related vars and PATH, so the real installed unit directory ends up empty and the label loses its suffix — I need to check what that implies for the daemon's runtime environment.

I also want to trace DaemonName resolution — it comes from watchPlan.DaemonName and falls back to the default name if unset, which was recorded by setup. And I confirmed the binary-change probe captures the initial stat before the watch loop starts, which looks correct. The key adversarial question now is whether that stale check actually fires in the real wedge scenario where the binary gets replaced while the daemon is running — it should trigger on the next polling pass within the configured interval.

The mtime equality check relies on build tools giving new mtimes; reproducible-build systems that preserve mtimes would instead be caught by the inode comparison for rename-based installs, though an in-place write with identical mtime, size, and inode would slip through — an edge case unlikely in practice. The SameFile comparison across separate stat calls checks device and inode correctly. I also note that if the initial stat fails, the probe returns nil and silently disables the staleness check, but since the path comes from os.Executable, that stat should reliably succeed.

Looking at spawnDetached, I'm checking that a nil plan.Env means the child inherits the daemon's full environment including PATH, so launchctl should be found as long as the daemon's PATH includes the standard system directories — though using an absolute path to launchctl would be more robust against minimal PATH edge cases. I'm also considering how uninstallDaemon now error-checks bootout, and thinking through what happens if the service isn't actually loaded when a user attempts to...

This matches old behavior so it's not a regression, maybe worth a nit about ignoring "not found" errors. Checking the retireRenamedDaemon flow and the install step's error handling for bootout/enable — these look consistent with the old implementation, and the Windows/Linux GUI domain quirk in tests doesn't matter since tests don't assert on it.

Looking at security: positional args avoid injection and plist paths are quoted properly. The relaunch helper's label and scope suffix match expectations, and the stale-check placement in the watch loop only happens between passes, so a long-running pass wouldn't catch a binary swap until the next cycle — that's acceptable.

Now I'm wondering what happens if the relaunch helper's bootstrap fails due to an invalid plist — the daemon would stay unregistered until setup runs again, and I'm checking whether that failure gets logged anywhere, but the helper's output goes to devnull since spawnDetached uses an empty LogPath.

I realize passing the actual daemon log path as LogPath would let helper failures get appended to watch.log, which seems like a real improvement worth noting. There's also a test gap: the wiring between runSupervisedWatch's sentinel handling and the relaunch call isn't covered, only the loop and probe individually. I'm also checking whether the stale-replacement error could fire incorrectly relative to the once-check, which looks fine since it's evaluated before that point, and considering whether the "registered but not running" detail message in daemonRunning reads correctly in the setup output context.

Continuing the adversarial pass, I'm verifying describeDaemonState's output, the no-register inspectDaemon detail text, the install/enable vs uninstall/disable ordering, and doc comment accuracy -- all look consistent. The bigger question is whether the probe genuinely addresses the ticket's "old daemon rejects manifest" scenario: it does catch binary replacement from a rebuild, but I need to think through what happens if the manifest itself comes from a newer build instead.

Imagining an edge case: if a developer runs a dev build of the binary manually while the daemon keeps running the old installed binary, the manifest gets rewritten with a new field but the daemon's binary is untouched, so ticks would keep failing with the same memory_state_corrupt classification even though status shows the daemon as healthily running. That's really the ticket's second fix direction -- reporting this as its own distinct error -- which I've decided is out of scope here.

I also double-check that the supervised loop always reaches the stale-check logic since it runs before plan loading, so no ordering bug there, and confirm the probe's one-shot behavior is consistent whether or not there's an installed daemon to maintain, including the nil-maintain case covered by tests.

There's a minor risk that the detached helper could bootout the daemon before the final log line prints, since the relaunch just spawns the helper and returns without waiting for the print to flush, but that's a small timing issue.

For the review itself, I'm planning to follow the repo's guidance to consult retained knowledge and run through the review-pr process plus the simplify skill — starting with a quick gh pr view/diff, then kicking off an independent reviewer in the background for a second pass.

After that I'll run the simplify skill, check how describeDaemonState renders details, then pull everything together into findings. Let me get started.

I'm suggesting hardening this with a small retry loop that attempts bootstrap a few times with short sleeps between tries. content.text:
`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change fixes the root cause at the right depth rather than
patching a symptom with a fragile bandaid. Special cases layered on shared
infrastructure are a sign the fix isn't deep enough — prefer the simpler, more
general change to the underlying mechanism over adding special cases, and name
that change.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

Looking at the reuse agent's findings, I'm weighing whether to dedupe the launchctl sequence by factoring the commands into a shared function, and considering swapping the hand-rolled daemon unit plan for the existing brainWatchDaemonPlanFor helper.

A deeper idea stands out: instead of using a shell script for the detached relaunch, I could have the new binary spawn itself with a hidden reinstall command that performs the daemon install under the registration lock, which would solve the locking concern too but requires adding a new hidden CLI flag.

But I realize the daemon itself can't re-register under the lock since bootout would kill it mid-call, and exec-ing the new binary into the same PID doesn't help since bootout still kills that PID. So the detached helper process really is necessary — the pragmatic path is factoring out the launchd registration argv triples into a shared helper that installDaemon can reuse.

For the GOOS invariant, I'll thread goos as a parameter into relaunchInstalledDaemon so the single-read-site rule stays intact while keeping it testable. The lock bypass concern (R3) is narrower than I thought — it's really just about the helper racing against concurrent setup, not a fundamental flaw.

The daemon registration lock can't be held across a shell child since there's no flock(1) on macOS by default, so wrapping the script won't work; I could route through a hidden internal cobra command, but that's scope creep for marginal benefit, so I'll just document the accepted race window and flag it in review as a known, bounded risk rather than engineering it away.

Tracing through the interleavings between setup's bootout/bootstrap and the helper's bootout/bootstrap, every ordering I can think of still ends with exactly one job registered — worst case there's a brief restart or a silent failure on the losing side, but the daemon always ends up running on the new binary, so the race is benign.

For the smaller items: the bytes.Contains check is trivial, I'll just apply it. I'm skipping the idea of collapsing the three install spawns into a shell call since the runner-recorded spawns are load-bearing for tests and shelling out would lose that. For merging the maintain and stale flags into a single upkeep struct, I'm weighing whether reducing the long parameter list of the supervised watch loop is worth the extra indirection.

I'm leaning toward skipping that merge too — log rotation and restart semantics are genuinely independent behaviors, and coupling them into one struct touches eight call sites for little real benefit. Moving to the probe signals, I want to keep SameFile and ModTime and I'm questioning whether Size is safe to drop, since mtime granularity can hide an in-place rewrite that happens within the same second, even on filesystems with nanosecond timestamps.

Thinking through `cp -p` style copies that preserve mtime over the same inode, Size is the only signal that would still catch a content change in that scenario, so it's cheap but not redundant — I'll keep it and note that it's a deliberate belt-and-suspenders choice rather than something to cut just to satisfy the reviewer's complexity concern.

For S4, I'll fold the os.Stat call into the daemon unit plan helper as part of the delegation refactor. I also want the helper to log to the daemon's watch.log so bootout/bootstrap failures are visible, print the "re-registering" line before spawning, and consider adding a small retry loop around bootstrap to handle the bootout→bootstrap teardown race now that logging will make failures observable.

Given the uncertainty around retry complexity, I'll keep it single-shot but logged for now and flag it as a watch-item rather than over-engineering it. The adversarial reviewer flags a potential race condition between the helper process and daemon uninstall: if a user runs uninstall while the helper is re-registering after a binary replacement, the interleaving could leave an orphaned job running with its plist already removed, persisting until logout.

I'm weighing a mitigation: having the helper verify the plist still exists right before calling bootstrap, which would shrink the race window to effectively nothing, especially since launchd actually reads the plist from disk at bootstrap time anyway — meaning a deleted plist would cause bootstrap to fail outright rather than succeed. That makes the orphan scenario require an even tighter sequencing than I first thought: uninstall's bootout and disable, then helper's enable and bootstrap while the plist still exists, then the plist removal — all within the same narrow window.

A simpler, lock-free fix occurs to me: just add a final bootout call in uninstall after the plist removal, acting as a belt-and-suspenders kill for any job that managed to re-register during that window, rather than overengineering checks inside the helper itself.

Now I'm shifting to a separate concern: even with this fix, machines already in a wedged state won't be rescued since their old daemon binary is still running stale code, and I need to check whether my planned environment-propagation changes actually address that.

Running through the setup logic, if the old daemon process is alive but just failing its ticks, `launchctl list` would still report it as Running, causing setup to skip reinstall entirely — so the live-wedged-process case never gets healed, unlike the spawn-failed case which does. To force a reinstall I'm considering bumping the unit material itself, since any rendered change to the plist contents (aside from PATH) would mark it as not-current and trigger a fresh install.

For systemd units I'd need the same trick — adding a revision comment line to the unit file, since the material comparison is just textual. The question is whether this one-time migration is worth it, given the affected population is really just machines currently wedged plus any that wedge between now and adopting this build; after that, the probe takes over for future cases.

Rechecking my daemonRunning fix against the wedged states: state A, daemon alive but ticks failing, still reports Running=true and skips — meaning the old daemon with no probe persists forever since setup just says "already running," the bug surviving its own fix for current victims. A revision bump forces one reinstall everywhere so everyone lands on a probed build — cheap, self-limiting, worth doing. I'll add a benign revision marker key into renderLaunchdPlist.

Instead of an unknown plist key, safer to use an XML comment like unit-revision markers, since plist and systemd parsers both ignore comments but my material-comparison code still includes them in its diff — so a bumped comment triggers drift and a one-time reinstall. entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

Five review findings against the previous commit, all fixed here:

  output, and re-derived the unit identity from environment the daemon

  concurrent `setup --uninstall-daemon` is left removed.

  a watcher installed into an overridden unit directory re-registers
  its own unit rather than resolving the default path.
- A rendered unit-revision comment forces one reinstall through the
  next `setup`: a wedged pre-probe daemon is alive, so it reports
  "already running" and would otherwise never be replaced by a build
  that can see its binary change.
- uninstall tolerates a job the service manager no longer lists:
  bootout fails for absence too, and absence is what uninstall wants.
- `daemonRunning` matches the PID entry with bytes.Contains instead of
  copying the whole launchctl payload into a string.

EOF

content.text:
# Review: PR #420 — daemon self-restart on binary replacement

Process: adversarial self-pass + independent correctness reviewer + 4 `/simplify` quality agents (reuse / simplification / efficiency / altitude). All findings verified against source; fixes landed as `8ac17755` and pushed.

## Findings — fixed in `8ac17755`

**[blocking] internal/cli/watch_binary.go — re-register helper could resurrect an uninstalled daemon.**
The `/bin/sh` helper ran outside `withDaemonRegistrationLock`, so its `enable`+`bootstrap` could interleave with a concurrent `setup --uninstall-daemon` and leave a running KeepAlive job with no unit file. **Fix:** the helper is now the replaced binary itself running a hidden `daemon-reregister` command that takes the registration lock and re-checks the unit file exists before reinstalling — a removed unit stays removed.

**[important] watch_binary.go — already-wedged daemons were never rescued.**
A wedged pre-probe daemon is *alive*, so `launchctl list` shows a PID, `setup` reports "already running," and the unit bytes were unchanged — the machines this PR exists for would never receive the fix. **Fix:** a rendered unit-revision comment changes the unit bytes once, so the next `setup` reads it as stale and reinstalls (`plutil -lint` confirms launchd still parses it).

**[important] watch_binary.go — wrong-unit targeting for scoped installs.**
The helper re-derived the unit path from `ENTIRE_BRAIN_DAEMON_DIR`, which `daemonEnv` never carried into the service — a daemon installed into an overridden directory would resolve (and bootout) the *default* plist. **Fix:** the variable is now propagated into the unit env, and plan derivation reuses `brainWatchDaemonPlan` instead of a hand-rolled copy (also restoring the "GOOS read in one place" invariant).

**[important] setup_daemon.go:649 — uninstall hard-failed on an already-unregistered job.**
`bootout` fails for absence too; uninstall then kept the plist. **Fix:** bootout failure is tolerated when `launchctl list` confirms the job is gone — the job's continued existence is the one portable error signal across macOS versions.

**[important] watch_binary.go — helper failures vanished into /dev/null.**
A failed bootstrap left the daemon unregistered with no trace. **Fix:** the re-register child logs to the daemon's own log file.

**[nit] setup_daemon.go:536 — PID check copied the full launchctl payload.** Now `bytes.Contains`.

## Findings — noted, deliberately not restructured

- **Helper vs concurrent `setup` races (reuse agent):** traced the interleavings — `bootstrap` is atomic check-and-register, so every ordering converges on exactly one registered job; the lock now held by the child narrows it further.
- **`maintain`/`stale` as separate loop params (simplification):** they gate on one condition in production, but folding them couples log rotation to restart semantics for 8 call sites of churn. Skipped.
- **Three-signal probe (simplification asked to drop one):** kept — `Size` catches mtime-preserving in-place copies (`cp -p`) that the other two miss.
- **Recording Label/UnitPath in the watch plan (altitude's deeper fix):** follow-up material — it adds a schema field with writer round-trip concerns, the exact failure class this ticket is about.
- **Residual gap (unchanged from PR body):** a daemon that *crashes* post-upgrade before its next pass stays down until `setup`/login.

## Summary

**Approve with the fixes applied** (done). The core design held up — both the independent reviewer and the altitude agent explicitly endorsed the probe-over-error-classification choice and the PID-based liveness fix. The original diff's real weaknesses were all in the detached helper: unlocked, silent, identity-guessing, and blind to already-wedged machines. All five are fixed, full `internal/cli` suite green, windows/linux cross-builds and `gofmt`/`vet` clean. Top remaining watch item: the first real nightly rollover is the live validation the sandbox can't provide — the bootout/bootstrap sequence is verified only by the ticket's manual repro.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_entire-prod-us__trail_findings
entries.description: Manage a trail's code-review findings (the CLI calls the same thing `entire trail finding`; the wire type is a review comment). list shows every finding on the trail, or scope it to one review with reviewId. get/update/create address a finding by trail + finding id alone — omit reviewId on get/update and the finding's owning review is found automatically; omit it on create and a review opens implicitly, the same two-step entire-api call the CLI's `finding add` makes as one. Also covers get_review (a review's own record) and files (the file content it covers). Mutating for update/create.

repo.description: the repository: a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, or git/<owner>/<repo>) or a 26-char repo ULID

action.description: list, get, update, create, get_review, or files

reviewId.description: review id; optional for list/get/update/create (see action docs), required for get_review/files

status.description: list: CSV filter open,resolved,dismissed; update: new status (one value) — resolved/dismissed require statusReason

severity.description: list: CSV filter high,medium,low; update: new severity (one value)

cursor.description: list: opaque cursor from a prior response's next_cursor

confidence.description: update: new confidence, 0-1 (0 is a valid value, distinct from omitting the field)

statusReason.description: update: reason; required when status becomes resolved or dismissed

content.text:
The failing tests are fixed and pushed (`40825efd`); a watcher is now waiting on the fresh CI run.

What was actually broken — one test, not the feature code:

- **`TestDaemonReregisterRespectsUninstall`** (added in the review-hardening commit) asserted `launchctl` verbs unconditionally, but `installedDaemonUnitPlan` resolves for the *host* service manager. On ubuntu the re-registration correctly ran `systemctl --user daemon-reload` / `enable --now` and the launchctl assertion failed; on Windows there is no supported manager, so `plan.UnitPath` is empty and the test's own unit-file write blew up ("The system cannot find the path specified").
- **Fix:** the test now asserts the host manager's verbs (launchd on darwin, systemd on linux) and, on unsupported platforms, stops after verifying the no-unit case is a calm no-op — which is the entire contract there.
- The other red checks were fallout, not independent failures: macOS was **cancelled** by fail-fast, `test (windows-latest)` and its coverage job just aggregate shard 0, and the Entire Gates "checks" gate mirrored CI. The gates on the new head now show only **approvals** blocking (needs one human review) plus the in-flight agent review (0 findings so far).

Validation: the fixed test passes on darwin, `GOOS=linux`/`GOOS=windows` typechecks pass, and the ubuntu CI log's recorded `systemctl` calls match my new assertions verbatim. I couldn't execute the linux test natively (Docker's VM OOM-killed compiling the sqlite dep), so the linux runtime confirmation is the CI run now in progress — I'll flag it if anything is still red when the watcher reports.

{"id":"COR-2174","uuid":"4b62e814-7dba-43b2-a2c9-7ac9a92be79d","title":"Upgrading entire-brain silently wedges the watch daemon: every tick fails, distill never runs, status says ✓ running","description":"## What happened

In `agent-insights`, `entire brain status` showed `facts 24/70 distilled (46 pending)` for about 18 hours with no progress, alongside `daemon ✓ running`.

* The launchd watch daemon (`io.entire.brain-watch.*`, running `entire-brain workspace watch --distill`) had been up since **2026-10-06**, so it was still executing that day's binary.
* `plugins/bin/entire-brain` was rebuilt and relinked on **2026-10-19** (nightly `0f23cbc2`). After <issue id="f14aab59-ddd8-41aa-ab69-109458b85980" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2168/entire-brain-stop-materializing-transcripts-manifest-driven">COR-2168</issue> (`245933e7`), that build writes `"transcript_storage"` into `manifest.json` but leaves `schema_version` at 3.
* Every daemon tick fails on every repo in the workspace:

```
[watch] refresh failed (skipping agent work this tick): parse brain manifest: memory_state_corrupt: brain manifest cannot be parsed: json: unknown field "transcript_storage"
```

* This appeared 120 times in `~/.local/state/entire/logs/watch.log`, across both repos in the default workspace.
* A failed refresh skips all agent work, so deferred sessions are never distilled. 38 sessions were deferred by `--max-sessions 25` on the first backfill, and new ones keep arriving.

## Why

1. **A long-running daemon outlives the binary it was started from.** Nothing restarts it when the binary changes (`KeepAlive` only covers process exit).
2. **The old daemon's refresh refuses the new manifest, and that refusal is correct.** `loadBrainManifestForReplace` (`internal/cli/brain.go`) intentionally rejects fields it can't round-trip so it doesn't erase another build's state. But the refusal is labeled `memory_state_corrupt` and treated as a per-tick failure. The daemon retries forever with no way to recover.
3. **Status hides it.** It reports the daemon as running (the process is alive) even though every tick has failed. `last_tick_at` for agent-insights is `0001-01-01T00:00:00Z`.

## Repro

1. Start the watch daemon on build A.
2. Rebuild or upgrade to build B, which adds a manifest field without a schema bump. Run any `entire brain` command once so B rewrites the manifest.
3. The daemon (still build A) fails every tick from then on, and `entire brain status` still shows `daemon ✓ running`.

## Workaround

`kickstart -k` **is not enough.** After it, launchd would not spawn the daemon at all: `launchctl print` showed `job state = spawn failed`, `last exit reason = OS_REASON_CODESIGNING`, `needs LWCR update`. launchd's managed launch constraint recorded the cdhash of the original ad-hoc-signed (`linker-signed`) binary, and the rebuilt binary has a different one. The binary itself passes `codesign --verify`.

What worked was re-registering the agent:

```
launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.entire.brain-watch.<hash>.plist
launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.entire.brain-watch.<hash>.plist
```

This matters for the "exit and let launchd restart" fix below: with an ad-hoc-signed binary that has changed, launchd won't relaunch it. The restart has to re-bootstrap the agent, or the binary needs a stable signing identity.

## Fix directions (pick, don't do all)

* The daemon notices that its executable changed on disk, or that the manifest was written by a newer build, and exits so launchd restarts it on the current binary. This is the simplest and fixes the root cause.
* Report "written by a newer build, restart required" as its own error, not as `memory_state_corrupt`.
* `status` shows the last tick's result or error rather than just process liveness. This overlaps with <issue id="1a788926-1147-4b77-89fd-873f38e120dc" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2162/a-component-stays-failed-after-the-cause-is-gone-and-two-status">COR-2162</issue>.","projectMilestone":{"id":"bc05f7ea-a603-4d11-bcdc-d9ef4afb9d74","name":"M2 Close the brain blockers"},"priority":{"value":2,"name":"High"},"url":"https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2174/upgrading-entire-brain-silently-wedges-the-watch-daemon-every-tick","gitBranchName":"evis/cor-2174-upgrading-entire-brain-silently-wedges-the-watch-daemon","createdAt":"2026-10-19T04:56:24.738Z","updatedAt":"2026-10-20T21:12:07.921Z","archivedAt":null,"completedAt":"2026-10-20T21:12:07.839Z","startedAt":"2026-10-20T18:56:11.319Z","canceledAt":null,"dueDate":null,"slaStartedAt":null,"slaMediumRiskAt":null,"slaHighRiskAt":null,"slaBreachesAt":null,"status":"Done","statusType":"completed","labels":["Bug"],"attachments":[{"id":"3d9d6b6a-6059-4e78-8f86-895e6fb8d9e6","title":"fix(watch): restart the supervised daemon when its binary is replaced","subtitle":null,"url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/420"}],"documents":[],"createdBy":"Alex Ong","createdById":"45a00cf6-3a37-45ab-a508-d9da7f9d514c","assignee":"Evis Drenova","assigneeId":"bd1c458e-3bb3-4d0c-8ad7-e36f19afc156","project":"P0 · GA the Local Brain","projectId":"91954c69-3fab-4281-84e0-cf4b81d85d75","team":"Core","teamId":"894690b6-2173-4cbe-abd3-6e7ea5ff5bb9"}

description.description: Content as Markdown. Do not escape the string — use literal newlines and special characters, not escape sequences. To mention a user, use @displayName (e.g., @johndoe)

patch.description: Partial edits applied to the current content, in order and atomically (one failing operation aborts the whole save). Every anchor string must match the current content exactly once. Only valid on update, in place of the full content/description field

old_string.description: Exact text to replace. Must match the current content exactly once

new_string.description: Replacement text. Empty string deletes the match

replace_all.description: Replace every occurrence instead of requiring a unique match

anchor.description: Exact text to insert before. Must match the current content exactly once

text.description: Text to insert directly before the anchor. Include separators (e.g. "\n\n")

anchor.description: Exact text to insert after. Must match the current content exactly once

text.description: Text to insert directly after the anchor. Include separators (e.g. "\n\n")
Text to insert at the very start of the content
Text to insert at the very end of the content

from.description: Exact text where the range starts (inclusive). Must match exactly once

to.description: Exact text where the range ends (exclusive, stays in place). Must match exactly once after `from`

new_string.description: Text replacing the range. Empty string deletes it

team.description: Team name or ID (required when creating)

template.description: Template name or ID. Applied on create only. The template fills in the content, fields, and sub-issues server-side. A `description` replaces the template body rather than merging with it, but an empty `description` keeps the template body. Labels merge with the template's own

cycle.description: Cycle name, number, or ID. Null to remove

project.description: Project name, ID, identifier (e.g., P-ENG-123), or slug. Null to remove

assignee.description: User ID, name, email, or "me". Null to remove

delegate.description: Agent name or ID. When the user asks to delegate to "Linear" or "the Linear agent", this refers to the "Linear" app user specifically. Null to remove

labels.description: Label names or IDs as a JSON array of strings (e.g. ["Bug", "Urgent"]). Replaces the full label set; existing labels not included are removed. Omit to leave labels unchanged. Cannot be combined with addLabels/removeLabels; prefer those for incremental changes

addLabels.description: Label names or IDs as a JSON array of strings (e.g. ["Bug", "Urgent"]) to add. Append-only; existing labels are never removed. Cannot be combined with a team change

removeLabels.description: Label names or IDs as a JSON array of strings (e.g. ["Bug", "Urgent"]) to remove. Only valid when updating an existing issue. Cannot be combined with a team change

dueDate.description: Due date (ISO format). On update, pass null to remove the due date

slaBreachesAt.description: ISO-8601 timestamp when the SLA will breach. On update, pass null to remove the SLA

slaType.description: SLA day counting type: "all" or "onlyBusinessDays". Only use with slaBreachesAt; null means unset

parentId.description: Parent issue ID or identifier (e.g., LIN-123). Null to remove

estimate.description: Issue estimate value. On create, pass null or omit for no estimate. On update, pass null to clear the estimate; omitting leaves it unchanged. 0 is a real estimate only on teams that allow zero estimates.

links.description: Link attachments to add [{url, title}]. Append-only; existing links are never removed

setReleases.description: Replace all releases on the issue with these. Cannot be combined with addReleases/removeReleases

addReleases.description: Release IDs or slugs to add. Append-only; existing releases are never removed

removeReleases.description: Release IDs or slugs to remove. Only valid when updating an existing issue

blocks.description: Issue IDs/identifiers this blocks. Append-only; existing relations are never removed

blockedBy.description: Issue IDs/identifiers blocking this. Append-only; existing relations are never removed

relatedTo.description: Related issue IDs/identifiers. Append-only; existing relations are never removed

duplicateOf.description: Duplicate of issue ID/identifier. Null to remove

removeBlockedBy.description: Issue IDs/identifiers to remove as blockers of this issue

input.body:
Fixed in PR #420 (merged as 5d79828c).

- The supervised daemon probes its executable each pass and exits when it was replaced; a detached `daemon-reregister` run of the new binary re-registers the launchd agent under the install lock, which re-records the cdhash pin (`bootout` → `enable` → `bootstrap`, the sequence verified above).
- `daemonRunning` now requires a PID entry in `launchctl list` output, so status reports "installed but not running" instead of "daemon ✓ running" for a dead job.
- A unit-revision comment in the rendered plist/unit forces one reinstall via the next `setup`, so daemons already wedged on a pre-fix build get replaced too.

Validated end-to-end on a sandboxed launchd agent: binary swapped under a running daemon, new daemon running the new build 19s later. The wedged daemon on this machine was repaired with `daemon-reregister`.

Known residual gap: a daemon that crashes after an upgrade but before its next pass stays down until `setup` runs or next login.
